``` ::: ::: ## Pooled cross-sections :::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Stacks one cross-section atop another - Also referred to as *repeated* cross-sections - Cannot follow the same individual through time. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Panels Follows the same units through time - Also referred to as *longitudinal* data - Here the data is shown in **wide** form; which is intuitive ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## :::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} For estimation, you need the data in **long** form (*akin to repeated cross-sections*) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Notation When we write down a linear regression model for a either a repeated cross-section or panel dataset, we add both $i$ and $t$ to the subscripts: $$ y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{it1} + \beta_2 x_{it2} + \dots + \beta_k x_{itk} + u_{it} $$ ::: {.fragment .fade-in} However, you may also have some variables that - do not vary with time: $x_{i}$ - e.g. individual ethnicity - vary only with time: $x_{t}$ - e.g. adding aggregate unemployment rate to individual level model of wages ::: # Pooled Cross-sections ## Example: Poverty & SCP Suppose, a researcher wants to evaluate the impact that of the [Home Energy Scotland Grant and Loan](https://www.homeenergyscotland.org/home-energy-scotland-grant-loan) programme on a household's energy expenditure. - Grant of up to £7,500 to install clean heating systems and energy efficiency measures. ![](material/lecture-9/home-energy-scotland.png){fig-align="center"} ## Empirical specification They propose the following linear regression model specification $$ energy_{it} = \delta + \beta grant_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma + \varepsilon_{it} $$ To be estimated using repeated cross-sections of the Scottish Household Survey. - $energy_{it}$: amount (£'s) spent on energy - $grant_{it}$: cumulative amount received from the programme ## Controls As controls, the author collects information at the household level ($\mathbf{x}_{it}$) on: 1. dwelling type 2. ownership type 3. household size 4. household income 5. number of rooms 6. location ## Time-varying factors But there are other key macroeconomics variables that explain expenditure on energy over time: 1. Global oil price 2. Exchange rate (GBP-USD) 3. Domestic energy prices (determined by domestic markets) This variables vary with time, but NOT across households: $$ \mathbf{z}_t\eta $$ ## So, our model is actually, $$ energy_{it} = \delta + \beta grant_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma + \mathbf{z}_t\eta + \varepsilon_{it} $$ where, - $\mathbf{x}$ includes household level controls - $\mathbf{z}$ includes time-varying (macroeconomic/aggregate) controls ## Identification Since the data comprises repeated cross-sections of individual, it is reasonable to assume that each observation is a random draw from the underlying population (MLR 2). \ - As before, we need MLR1-4a for consistency. - The question is more whether MLR 1 holds true across time. - Is the model time-invariant? ## Time-varying parameters We could evaluate this question using a Chow test: - Estimate the model separately for each year: $$ energy_{is} = \delta_s + \beta_s grant_{is} + \mathbf{x}_{is}\gamma_s + \mathbf{z}_s\eta_s + \varepsilon_{is} \quad \text{for}\;s = 1,\dots,T $$ - Test whether the parameters vary using $SSR_s$ from each equation. ## **BUT** there is a problem here for $\mathbf{z}_s\eta_s$ in the model: - In any given period, these variables do not vary - e.g., if oil price is \$100 (per barrol) for period $s=1$ and \$120 (per barrol) for period $s=2$ - but within a given period $t$, the oil price doesn't vary across households. - So, $\mathbf{z}_s\eta_s$ is a constant! And cannot be separately identified from $\delta_s$, the time-varying constant. ## Time fixed effects If we take our original model and allow the constant term (only) to vary with time. $$ energy_{it} = \delta_t + \beta grant_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma + \varepsilon_{it} $$ then we must exclude all variables that also vary *only* with time: $\mathbf{z}_t\eta$ - We call $\delta_t$ **time fixed effects** - These time FEs "absorb" any other variables that vary only with time. - We say, time FEs "control" for any time-varying (e.g., macroeconomic) factors/shocks; **even ones we don't observe** in the data. ## Time dummies: When it comes to estimation, time FEs are equvilent to including a set of dummy variables: one for each year. $$ \begin{aligned} energy_{it} =& \delta_t + \beta grant_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma + \varepsilon_{it} \\ =& \sum_{s=1}^{T}\delta_s \mathbf{1}\{s=t\} + \beta grant_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma + \varepsilon_{it} \end{aligned} $$ In place of a constant, we have $T$ dummy variables that identify each period. For any given $t$, only one of these dummies $=1$ :::{.callout-note} This notation can be very confusing. Do not concern yourself with the complicated sum, but rather the intuition that when we include an intercept in a linear regression it gives us the slope coefficient on a constant (a regressor that $=1$ for all observations). To implement time FEs, we are essentially adding a separate constant for each period. And these constants are all just dummy variables: $\mathbf{1}\{s=t\}$. ::: ## In Stata/R # Panel Models ## Preamble There is a large, complex literature on panel data models: - Static vs Dynamic models - Short (small $T$) vs long (large $T$) panels - Variance (standard error) corrections for autocorrelation We are going to skip over many of these topics, to talk about the types of panel data models you might see in modern applied (microeconomic) research - short, static panel data models ## Identification We are going to discuss an estimation procedure that deals with potential endogeneity of error term related to time-invariant heterogeneity ($\nu_{i}$): $$ \varepsilon_{it} = \nu_{i}+\upsilon_{it} $$ for example, $\nu_{i}$ may reflect unobserved preferences within a household w.r.t. heating fo the home. - Likely that $E[\nu_{i}|grant_{it},\mathbf{x}_{it},\mathbf{x}_{i}]\neq 0$ ## Covariance But there is also an issue regarding correlation of $\varepsilon_{it}$ across observations. - Suppose we deal with $\nu_{i}$ - We must expect that $$ Cov(\upsilon_{it},\upsilon_{is}) \neq 0 \quad \text{for}\; t\neq s $$ - Issue for estimation of variance. - We fix this by estimating clustered SEs (at the unit level) ## Example Consider our model: $$ energy_{it} = \delta_t + \beta grant_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma + \varepsilon_{it} $$ Some of the household characteristics in $\mathbf{x}_{it}$ may not vary with time: 1. dwelling type (might not) 2. ownership type (might not) 3. household size (might not) 4. household income (probably does) 5. number of rooms (might not) 6. location (might not) **What really matters is whether they vary in the data.** ## Time-invarianct covariates Let's split up the household characteristics into - those that vary with time: $\mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma_1$ - those that are time-invariant: $\mathbf{x}_{i}\gamma_2$ $$ energy_{it} = \delta_t + \beta grant_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma_1 + \mathbf{x}_{i}\gamma_2 + \varepsilon_{it} $$ ## Unit FEs Because we observe repeated observations of the **same** household, we can include unit FEs $$ energy_{it} = \alpha_i + \delta_t + \beta grant_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma_1 + \varepsilon_{it} $$ **BUT** by the same logic as before, - unit FEs "absorb" anything that is invariant at the unit level: $\mathbf{x}_{i}\gamma_2$ - we say, unit FEs "control" for any time-invariant (e.g., fixed building characteristics) heterogeneity (i.e. things that vary across $i$); **even ones we don't observe** in the data. - unit FEs potentially control for things we do not observe: e.g. household preferences over how warm to keep their home. ## Time-varying treatment Crucially, this means that the treatment variable $grant_{it}$ must vary at the **unit-level over time**. $$ energy_{it} = \alpha_i + \delta_t + \beta grant_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}\gamma_1 + \varepsilon_{it} $$ for example, a households (cumulative) grant is looks like over 4 periods $$ grant_{i} = \{0,0,3000,7500\} $$ ## Estimation The OLS estimator for this model is often referred to as the "fixed-effects" (or "within") estimator. The logic is that you estimate a transformed version of the model: $$ \widetilde{energy}_{it} = \delta_t + \beta \widetilde{grant}_{it} + \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{it}\gamma_1 + \tilde{\varepsilon}_{it} $$ where each variable has been demeaned at the **unit-level** $$ \widetilde{energy}_{it} = energy_{it} - \overline{energy}_{i} $$ - Remember: when you include a constant in the model it does the same thing, but using the global mean of the variable. - Helps with the intuition of why the remaining variables must vary at the unit level over time. ## In Stata/R

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
